title: Boundary Embedding Shaping for Cleaner Decisions
one_liner: When a graph model reads node labels, it learns from neighbor noise worst near class boundaries — this paper fixes the boundary noise, not the whole graph.
lead: A graph model learns which nodes are in which class by reading information from nearby nodes. The problem: neighbors sometimes send misleading signals — false positives mixed in with real ones. This noise hits hardest where the model is uncertain, right at the boundary between two classes. This paper identifies that boundary-zone noise as the main bottleneck and fixes it directly, keeping most of the model unchanged.

problem.h2: The bottleneck: noise at decision boundaries
paras: A graph neural network predicts a node's class by looking at that node's neighbors. Each neighbor sends a signal: this node looks like class A or class B. The model adds up these signals and makes a guess.

Spurious neighbors exist — they send wrong signals. A node that happens to sit next to a class B node, even though it is actually class A, picks up that misleading signal. The model's learned representation of that node (called an embedding, a list of numbers that captures the node's identity) gets contaminated with noise.

This noise does not hurt equally everywhere. When the model is confident — the signals pile up clearly on one side — a bit of noise washes out. But nodes sitting near the boundary between classes, where the signals are already close and pushing from both sides, are fragile. A little extra noise tips the balance. The model gets the call wrong more often here.

callout.html: Treat every node the same: use the standard graph model, accept all neighbor signals as equally real.

steps.text: Find nodes whose embeddings sit near the decision boundary between classes.
For each boundary node, score which neighbors send useful signals and which are misleading.
Use pairs of examples to teach the model which signals should be pulled together and which pushed apart.

steps.b: Suppress spurious signals for boundary nodes only
steps.text: Reduce the weight of misleading neighbor signals, but only for nodes near the decision line.
Embeddings shift to be closer to their true class and farther from false neighbors.

paras: The graph model's neighbor-reading step. Normally every neighbor signal gets treated the same. BES adds a gate: for boundary nodes, some neighbor signals are muted. The gate adapts per node, so boundary nodes learn to suppress the spurious ones without changing the model's core structure.

hidden.name: structural noise intensity at decision boundary
paras: This is the amount of misleading information nodes receive from spurious neighbors, measured strongest at the decision boundary where it causes the most misclassification. It is not a fixed property of the graph — it depends on where the model's decision boundary sits in the embedding space at that moment.

BES estimates this quantity by measuring, for each boundary node, how many neighbors belong to the opposite class and how strongly they pull the embedding toward the wrong direction. The paper uses adaptive contrastive learning to measure and track this, then reduces it.

heat.caption: Darker means more spurious neighbor signals; marked cells are at decision boundaries where they do the most harm.

reads.html: Spurious neighbors are nodes from the opposite class that happen to connect to your node in the graph. The stronger their pull (the more they disagree with your true class), and the closer you sit to the decision boundary, the more danger they pose, because boundary nodes already have balanced signals from both classes and cannot absorb additional wrong signals without tipping toward the wrong class.

BES computes a contrastive loss that pulls same-class neighbors close and pushes spurious neighbors away, weighted by boundary proximity. The weight is high for nodes whose embeddings sit near the decision surface.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: focused intervention at the weakest point
paras: Graph models aggregate signals from neighbors. If a node sits firmly in one class region, noise from a few spurious neighbors drowns out — the overwhelming signal from true-class neighbors keeps it stable. But a boundary node is already torn between two directions. Spurious signals there are lethal: they push it over the edge into the wrong class.

BES works by recognizing this asymmetry. Instead of trying to fix spurious neighbors everywhere (expensive and risky), it focuses: identify which nodes sit at the boundary, and for those nodes only, suppress the misleading neighbor signals. This is done via contrastive learning — pairs of nodes teach the model which neighbors are trustworthy and which are not.
The key is adaptivity: the model learns which neighbors are spurious for each boundary node, because spurious changes as embeddings move. The gate is part of the model, not a fixed filter.

stages.s: Node and its neighbors in the graph
Compute node embedding using neighbor signals (standard aggregation)
Check if embedding sits near decision boundary
If at boundary: suppress neighbor signals that point toward wrong class
If in interior: use all signals (standard)
Cleaner node embedding, pushed toward correct class

math.words: For a boundary node, the total penalty is: standard aggregation plus a contrastive term that pulls same-class neighbors close and pushes different-class neighbors away, weighted by boundary distance.
symbols: total loss for a boundary node
how strong the contrastive correction is (a dial to turn up or down)
how close neighbors of the same class are in the embedding
how far away different-class neighbors are
a score from 0 to 1: how close to the decision line (high for boundary nodes, low for interior)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Boundary node X sits very close to the decision boundary, proximity score 0.9.
Standard aggregation gives embedding loss L_agg = 0.5.
Same-class neighbors are 0.2 away in embedding space, different-class neighbors are 0.4 away.
Contrastive penalty: D_same_class (0.2) + D_diff_class (0.4) = 0.6. (We want same-class close, different-class far.)
Compare to interior node Y, proximity 0.1: total loss = 0.5 + 2.0 * 0.6 * 0.1 = 0.5 + 0.12 = 0.62.
Same embedding quality issues, but boundary node gets 1.5x more correction because it is vulnerable.

math.note: The formula says: boundary nodes get the most aggressive correction, because they sit where spurious neighbors do the most damage.

bars.h2: What a standard GNN does versus BES

charts.title: Standard graph neural network
charts.note: Boundary nodes suffer. Interior nodes do fine.

charts.title: With BES boundary fixing
charts.note: Boundary accuracy rises from 72 to 85 because suppressing spurious signals lets the true class signal dominate. Interior stays at 94-95 because those nodes already had overwhelming signals from their true class and the contrastive correction is low-weight there. Overall improves 7 points because the boundary node improvement outweighs any small change elsewhere.

items.html: If the model misidentifies which nodes sit at the boundary — e.g., because the initial embeddings are very noisy — it suppresses signals for the wrong nodes and makes things worse.
If lambda (the contrastive strength) is set too high, the model over-corrects and starts throwing out useful neighbor signals at the boundary, losing real information.
If one class is much rarer than the other, spurious neighbors are biased toward the common class, and the paper does not directly address that asymmetry.

When lambda is tuned so that contrastive correction is strong enough to filter noise but weak enough to keep good signals, and when the boundary detection is accurate, BES cleanly lifts boundary-node accuracy without hurting interior nodes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple graph with two clear classes and a few spurious edges connecting them. Train a standard GNN and measure accuracy separately for nodes at the boundary versus nodes in the interior. Then train with BES and measure again. Show that: (1) boundary nodes improve more than interior nodes, because BES suppresses spurious signals specifically there; (2) interior accuracy stays about the same or improves, because BES applies little correction weight to interior nodes; (3) the decision boundary in embedding space becomes sharper and cleaner, because boundary nodes are less scattered by spurious signals and stay clustered with their true class.
demo.closing: The demo must make clear that BES is not a general noise filter — it is a laser focused on the one place noise matters most, the decision boundary.
